# Research

My research lies at the intersection of industrial organization, international trade, and macroeconomics. I study how firm-level behavior and market power shape welfare and aggregate outcomes.
:::

## Job Market Paper {#job-market-paper}

::: {.paper-list}
::: {.paper-item}
<span class="status">Job market paper</span>

### Market Power and Firm-Level Welfare Incidence

<p class="authors">Sébastien Lamproye</p>

<p class="abstract">Which firms’ markup changes matter most for aggregate welfare costs? I derive marginal and finite measures of firm-level welfare incidence in a parsimonious static model that accounts for fixed-cost recovery. The method uses company accounts and calibrated demand elasticities, without requiring firm-level prices or physical quantities. Belgian company accounts for 1985–2024 reveal highly concentrated effects and firm rankings that differ substantially from those based on sales, markups or profitability. These effects evaluate separate firm-level changes and need not sum to the aggregate welfare cost of markups.</p>

<div class="paper-links"><a href="papers/Lamproye_JMP.pdf">Read paper (PDF)</a><span>Updated 4 November 2026</span></div>
:::
:::

## Working Papers

<span class="status">Forthcoming NBB Working Paper</span>

### Aggregating Markups in Production Networks

<p class="authors">with <a href="https://orbi.umons.ac.be/profile?uid=501113">Emmanuel Dhyne</a> (National Bank of Belgium and University of Mons)</p>

<p class="abstract">How should firm-level markups be aggregated when production takes place through input–output networks? We derive an aggregate markup consistent with household incidence and show how cost-based exposure weights trace distortions through the production network. We bring the framework to near-universe Belgian firm-to-firm data.</p>

<div class="paper-links"><a href="papers/Lamproye_Dhyne_Aggregating_Markups.pdf">Read paper (PDF)</a><span>22 April 2026</span></div>
:::

::: {.paper-item}
<span class="status">Forthcoming NBB Working Paper</span>

### Market Power and Firm-Level Welfare Impact in Production Networks

<p class="authors">with <a href="https://orbi.umons.ac.be/profile?uid=501113">Emmanuel Dhyne</a> (National Bank of Belgium and University of Mons)</p>

<p class="abstract">Which firms matter most for the welfare cost of market power in a production network? We map firm-level markups and firm-to-firm linkages into aggregate welfare losses and firm-level welfare effects, then implement the framework using Belgian administrative transaction data.</p>

<div class="paper-links"><a href="papers/Lamproye_Dhyne_Welfare_Impact_Networks.pdf">Read paper (PDF)</a><span>18 June 2026</span></div>
:::

:::

## Under Review

<span class="status">Revise and resubmit at <em>Economics of Innovation and New Technology</em></span>

### Technological Knowledge Intensity and Intergenerational Mobility across U.S. Regions

<p class="authors">Sébastien Lamproye</p>

<p class="abstract">This paper studies the regional relationship between technological knowledge intensity and intergenerational upward mobility in the United States. Combining regional income-mobility estimates with U.S. patent records, I document that regions with greater patent-based knowledge intensity exhibit higher upward mobility.</p>

<div class="paper-links"><a href="papers/Lamproye_Technological_Knowledge_Mobility.pdf">Read paper (PDF)</a><span>Submitted version · 31 May 2026</span></div>
:::

::: {.paper-item}
<span class="status">Submitted</span>

### Equal Static Gains, Unequal Growth: Trade and the Allocation of R&D

<p class="authors">Sébastien Lamproye</p>

<p class="abstract">Can trade reforms that deliver the same current real-income gain have opposite effects on long-run growth? This paper studies firms’ R&D choices when sectors compete for a fixed national supply of research labor. It derives an equal-static-gain growth frontier and quantifies the mechanism in a multi-country, multi-sector model with input–output linkages.</p>
:::

::: {.paper-item}
<span class="status">Submitted</span>

### When Comparison Makes Markets Tip

<p class="authors">with <a href="https://sites.google.com/view/phan-dda/welcome">Duy-Anh Phan</a> (Monash University)</p>

<p class="abstract">Policies that make platforms easier to compare are expected to lower prices. This paper shows that, in two-sided markets, greater comparability can also strengthen participation feedback and destabilize coexistence. It distinguishes comparison policies from interventions that weaken network feedback, such as interoperability and multi-homing support.</p>

<div class="paper-links"><a href="https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=6489378">Read on SSRN</a></div>
:::

:::
